Chapter 1: Rethinking Praise and Motivation in Children
Picture this: a child sits at the kitchen table, pencil clutched tight, brow furrowed in deep concentration over a math worksheet.
A parent, wanting to help, leans in and says, “You’re so smart!”
On the surface, those words are meant to lift the child up, to build confidence and offer reassurance.
But have you ever wondered what’s really happening underneath?
Sure, that praise sparks a little glow in the moment.
But the next time a tough problem comes along?
Suddenly, hesitation creeps in. What if the answer doesn’t come so easily this time?
What if being “smart” just isn’t enough?
For years, we’ve been told that kids thrive on praise. We hand out compliments about intelligence or talent, hoping to boost self-esteem and encourage achievement.
But as research has dug deeper, it turns out that praising innate ability doesn’t always lead where we hope.
In classrooms and at home, the effects of praise are more complicated than they seem. When a child hears, “You’re so smart,” it can start to feel like intelligence is just something you have—or don’t.
And when that belief takes hold, challenges become risks.
Kids start avoiding tough assignments, worried about losing that “smart” label if they mess up.
It’s a quiet burden—one that shapes their choices and can even hold them back.
There’s a story that really brings this to life. Imagine a teacher noticing how some students, after being praised for their intelligence, shy away from difficult tasks. They stick to what’s safe, what almost guarantees success.
Now, compare that to students who hear, “You worked really hard on that.”
Those kids? They’re more willing to dive into tough problems.
They don’t see mistakes as a sign of failure, but as a part of learning—proof that they’re growing.
The real difference is what the praise is shining a light on. When we focus on effort, kids start to believe that persistence and hard work actually help them improve.
They bounce back from setbacks, try again, and get more out of the process.
So, what does this mean for parents and teachers?
Well, it’s something we all wrestle with. The urge to protect a child’s self-esteem is natural, but real resilience and motivation grow when kids see value in trying, struggling, and learning from mistakes.
It’s not about never praising them—it’s about choosing words that help them develop a growth mindset.
Here’s the simple, but powerful, lesson: Children flourish when we recognize their effort, not just their natural ability.
Confidence and achievement don’t come from avoiding mistakes—they come from persistence, curiosity, and the freedom to learn along the way.
In the end, it’s not about being smart.
It’s about becoming smarter, one challenge at a time.
